title: The First Step For Network Marketing Success
summary: Network-marketing motivational talk: the one secret is an irreversible decision to go to the top, with no plan B.

assertions.quote: That moment when you burn your bridges. That moment when you eliminate all your escape plans

verdicts.note: Commitment does not change the structural payout; income disclosures show nearly all participants lose regardless of effort.

Hours worked correlated equally with profits (r=0.27) and with losses (r=0.27), and money invested likewise with both, so the authors conclude success or failure in MLM cannot be determined by how hard a person works; effort is the proxy for commitment here.

Taylor devoted all his time to Nu Skin for a year, reached the top 1% of participants, spent over $1,500 a month and earned about $250 a month in commissions, netting a $15,000 loss; full commitment did not produce success.

assertions.quote: If somebody in your company has gone all the way the top that means you can to.

verdicts.note: Top ranks are a fraction of a percent by construction; the position depends on recruiting timing, not just skill.

Model conclusion: the most successful agents are almost never the most talented but those near average talent who happened to be luckiest, so one person reaching the top is evidence of their luck rather than of a path others can follow; environment (share of lucky events) also strongly affects outcomes.

64 of 70 disclosures attribute success to hard work or skill, but the FTC finds no basis given that these qualities distinguish successful from unsuccessful participants, and none acknowledges that saturation or lack of demand can constrain earnings regardless of effort.
Only 3 of 601 participants (0.5%) reported $100,000+ in profit, all after 5+ years and one as the company founder, while neither hours nor money invested separated winners from losers.

Top-loaded MLM pay plans transfer the investments of the latest recruits to the earliest ones, so the vast majority are always at the bottom where profit is impossible; who reached the top depends on when they joined, not background.

assertions.quote: I made the decision to walk away from lucky.

verdicts.note: Sales and recruiting skills matter at the margin, but the pyramid structure caps how many can profit.

Generic simulation, not network marketing: talent is necessary but almost never sufficient, with the highest-talent agents topping the success ranking in only 3% of runs, so skill alone does not explain who reaches the top.

Disclosures routinely state that income depends on skill, effort and leadership, but the FTC says it is not apparent what basis exists for the claim that those qualities drive success; the source cannot say whether skill or luck decides outcomes.

The UK Amway judgment quoted by Taylor found the thin top of the income 'candlestick' was those who had been IBOs longest (since 1979), while recent joiners and many long-term IBOs formed the base; position in the chain, not skill, drives outcomes.
True that it is not quick; the omission is that years of effort still leave most participants with a loss.
One disclosure states its top 1% of earners averaged 8 years (range 1-11) to get there, supporting that the top takes years; one company's figure, and it says nothing about skill-building.

The only three participants reporting $100,000+ in profit had all worked the MLM for more than 5 years (one over 20), but 44% of participants quit within a year and most never profit, so years of effort are necessary, not sufficient.

Taylor agrees MLM plans do not reward part-time or short effort and that profiting requires aggressive long-term recruitment, but adds that only a tiny few ever recruit enough to profit even with years of effort.
